summary: Spacecraft propulsion traditionally relies on volatile fuels and separate, bulky systems for different types of maneuvering in space. NASA is working to change that paradigm. body: Spacecraft propulsion traditionally relies on volatile fuels and separate, bulky systems for different types of maneuvering in space. NASA is working to change that paradigm. Engineers at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, recently completed a rigorous series of environmental and physical tests on a new small satellite designed to make spaceflight safer and more efficient. The ASCENT (Advanced Spacecraft Energetic Non-Toxic) Propulsion Dual Mode mission is a flight demonstration of a spacecraft about the size of a large shoebox. The mission will test a single, integrated propulsion system that uses a common fuel tank to feed two different types of engines. Dr. Nehemiah Williams, the demonstration’s project manager at NASA, prepares to start testing the mission’s flight hardware in a clean room at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. The mission will demonstrate a single, non-toxic propulsion system that combines both high-thrust and low-thrust capabilities into a common tank. title: Here’s what Magic Pointer processes on your Googlebook — and what goes online
summary: Screen recognition stays local until you ask Gemini to act.
body: TL;DR Magic Pointer identifies things you can interact with on your Googlebook screen locally after you activate it. Once you select something and ask Gemini to act on it, it sends the content to a cloud model. Google says the AI cursor stays inactive until you deliberately trigger it. Google looked at one of the oldest parts of the desktop experience — the mouse cursor — and decided Gemini could make it useful for more than clicking things. The result is Magic Pointer, which can understand whatever you highlight on a Googlebook and help you act on it. That sounds incredibly handy, but it also raises a pretty important privacy question: when exactly does what’s on your screen leave your laptop and head to Google’s cloud? Google has now explained where that line sits. Speaking on Android Faithful , Alexander Kuscher, Google’s Senior Director of Product for Laptops and Tablets, broke down what happens behind the scenes when you use Magic Pointer.

title: ARMSX3 PS3 emulator can finally run games at playable frame rates with new update
summary: ARMSX3 is slowly becoming a real candidate for PS3 emulation on Android.
body: TL;DR The ARMSX3 PS3 emulator just got a major update that fixes game crashes and adds several features. It can now run games at playable frame rates, including Helldivers and Race the Sun at 60fps. It also supports PS3 themes, SIXAXIS motion controls, multi-game discs, and more. When the team behind the popular PS2 emulator ARMSX2 launched its PS3 emulator , it was just a proof of concept. As such, it had several issues, including the fact that most games didn’t run at a playable frame rate. Now, the devs have released an update that brings several improvements, including useful tweaks to touch controls. The update was announced in a Reddit post detailing a laundry list of improvements to the emulator. ARMSX3 now supports PS3 themes as library backgrounds. Users can set up pictures, slideshows, animated themes, and full 3D scenes that play live in the library background. According to the devs, they tested the feature with 92 dynamic themes, and each one played properly.

body: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR Pixel Watch 3 and newer models are receiving the promised Health Guardian features. These include blood pressure and insulin resistance trends, as well as sleep quality analysis. The features are now available for free on the Pixel Watch, while Fitbit Air users will have to pay for them. title: Gmail is turning its stars and importance markers blue, and users aren’t happy

body: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR Google replaced Gmail’s default yellow stars and yellow importance chevrons with high-contrast, saturated blue markers to improve accessibility. However, users complain that the identical blue tones flatten the visual hierarchy, make email scanning harder, and add visual clutter. While there’s no way to revert the changes, you can manually select a yellow star preset (and re-star items) or hide importance chevrons entirely in Settings. Google is rolling out a visual overhaul to Gmail on the web, replacing its longstanding yellow stars and importance markers with a bright, high-contrast blue. While Gmail has gained plenty of genuinely practical upgrades recently, such as letting you copy 2FA codes directly without opening emails or leveraging AI overview search capabilities , this particular color switch has annoyed desktop users who rely on quick visual cues to scan their messages. In a post on X , the official Gmail team confirmed the change, explaining that it updated the default star and “Important” label colors from yellow to blue to meet modern accessibility standards and ensure inboxes are easier to read and more inclusive.
